findings_qualitative.value: The protostellar envelope is traced by C18O, DCO+, and N2D+, with CO freeze-out governing the chemistry at envelope scales (N2D+ peaks offset from continuum where CO is frozen out, while DCO+ peaks near the CO snowline).

evidence.quote: The protostellar envelope is well traced by C [18] O, DCO [+] and N 2 D [+], with the freeze-out of CO governing the chemistry at envelope scales.

As DCO [+] requires gas-phase CO for its formation, it peaks close to the CO snowline, which is within the resolution of our observations (∼1800–2500 au radius), while N 2 D [+] is only located where CO is not present in the gas phase.

findings_qualitative.value: Extremely high-velocity (EHV) molecular jets are detected in 6 out of 7 Class 0 sources (including new detections in B1-c and SMM3, and a third known H2CO bullet in SMM3) and are absent in Class I sources.

evidence.quote: What is especially important to highlight is the third detection of a H 2 CO bullet in SMM3 after IRAS 04166 (Tafalla et al. 2010) and Emb8N (Tychoniec et al. 2019).

evidence.loc: 4.7. Class 0 vs Class I in different components
evidence.quote: In our sample 6 out of 7 sources have high-velocity component and none is detected in Class I (Section 4.2.1)

findings_qualitative.value: Outflow cavity walls in Class 0 protostars are traced by UV-irradiation tracers (C2H, c-C3H2, CN) and high-density tracers (13CS, H13CO+).

evidence.quote: To summarize, we observe the hydrocarbons C 2 H and c-C 3 H 2, as well as CN, H [13] CO [+] and [13] CS in the outflow cavity walls of Class 0 protostars.

findings_qualitative.value: In Class I disks, C17O traces the disk midplane whereas CN traces the upper irradiated layers of the disk and residual cavity walls/winds.

evidence.quote: In comparison with the C [17] O emission, which traces the midplane disk, CN thus appears in the upper layers and in the outflow, therefore in most cases the two molecules are mutually exclusive.

findings_qualitative.value: COMs and small hydrocarbons (C2H, c-C3H2) coexist in the same protostellar sources, with COMs tracing the hot core and outflows and hydrocarbons tracing the UV-irradiated cavity walls.

evidence.quote: COMs can coexist with hydrocarbons in the same protostellar sources, but they trace different components.
Hydrocarbons and COMs are found to co-exist routinely in protostellar sources: the former are present in the UV-irradiated cavity walls and the latter in the hot core and in the outflows.

claims.hypothesis: Specific simple and complex molecules can be used to uniquely diagnose the distinct physical components (envelope, jet, outflow, cavity walls, hot core, disk) of Class 0 and Class I protostellar systems.
claims.experiment: Analyze multi-band (Bands 3, 5, 6) ALMA 12m and ACA 7m maps and spectra of 16 Class 0 and Class I protostars across low- and high-excitation transitions.
claims.result: Distinct spatial and kinematic morphologies are identified: C18O, DCO+, and N2D+ trace the envelope; high-velocity CO, SiO, SO, and H2CO trace jets; low-velocity CO, SiO, SO, HCN, and sputtered COMs trace outflows; C2H, c-C3H2, CN, and 13CS trace cavity walls; compact COMs and S-bearing species trace hot cores; C17O and CN trace Class I disk midplanes and upper layers.
claims.finding: Sub-arcsecond millimeter-wave observations combined with larger-scale data successfully identify the key molecular tracers for each physical component and their evolutionary changes from Class 0 to Class I.

evidence.quote: Sub-arcsecond millimeter-wave observations allow to identify those (simple) molecules that best trace each of the physical components of a protostellar system.

claims.hypothesis: COMs released by non-thermal shock sputtering in outflows have comparable relative abundances to COMs thermally sublimated in the hot core, or show differences indicative of gas-phase chemistry.
claims.experiment: Extract spectra in 3'' regions in the blueshifted and redshifted outflow lobes of S68N, compute LTE column densities relative to CH3OH using CASSIS, and compare with hot core ratios from van Gelder et al. (2020) and Nazari et al. (2021).
claims.result: Relative abundances of COMs with respect to CH3OH are very similar in both outflow lobes and generally comparable to the S68N hot core, except for CH3CHO and H2CCO which are enhanced in the outflow.
claims.finding: COMs are found in both the hot inner envelope and outflows with mostly comparable abundances, while the enhancement of CH3CHO and H2CCO in the outflow may be attributed to additional gas-phase formation in shocks.

evidence.quote: COMs are found both in the hot inner envelope (high excitation lines) and in the outflows (lower-excitation lines) with comparable abundances.

evidence.loc: 4.5. COMs in outflow versus hot core
evidence.quote: Second, most abundances relative to CH 3 OH are found to be comparable to the S68N hot core within our uncertainties and those of van Gelder et al. (2020) and Nazari et al. (2021)

evidence.loc: 4.5. COMs in outflow versus hot core
evidence.quote: The greatest difference is seen for CH 3 CHO and H 2 CCO, which could be attributed to the additional gas-phase formation in shocks.

claims.hypothesis: The presence of small hydrocarbons (C2H, c-C3H2) requires warm carbon-chain chemistry (WCCC) and is mutually exclusive with hot core COMs.
claims.experiment: Map small hydrocarbons (C2H, c-C3H2) and COMs at 0.5'' resolution in Class 0 protostars such as B1-c, S68N, and SMM3.
claims.result: Small hydrocarbons and COMs are detected in the same sources, with hydrocarbons spatially confined to the UV-irradiated outflow cavity walls and COMs located in the central hot core and outflow.
claims.finding: COMs and small hydrocarbons routinely coexist in the same protostars; PDR chemistry in UV-irradiated cavity walls is sufficient to explain C2H and c-C3H2 without invoking WCCC.

evidence.loc: 4.6. Carbon-chains and other hydrocarbons vs COMs
evidence.quote: Our data also show detection of small hydrocarbons and COMs in the same sources (Fig. 14).

evidence.loc: 4.6. Carbon-chains and other hydrocarbons vs COMs
evidence.quote: Both c-C 3 H 2 and C 2 H can be solely explained by PDR chemistry (Guzmán et al. 2015; Cuadrado et al. 2015) even in moderate UV fields of low-mass protostars and therefore WCCC chemistry does not need to be invoked for the sources presented in this work.

why_this_data.value: Combining ALMA 12m (Bands 3, 5, 6 at 0.3''-3'') and ACA 7m (Band 6 at 6'') provides both low- and high-excitation lines and preserves sensitivity from sub-arcsecond inner envelope/disk scales (35-110 au) to large envelope scales (800-2000 au, MRS up to 30'').

evidence.quote: The availability of both low- and high-excitation lines, as well as data on small and larger scales, are important to unravel the full picture.
The ALMA observations presented here target different spectral setups across Band 3, 5, and 6. This allows to probe the strongly varying physical scales and conditions.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Top-down destruction of PAHs as the formation route for small hydrocarbons in cavity walls (rejected because PAHs are rare in low-mass protostars and require UV fields > 10^3 G0).

evidence.quote: The top-down production of hydrocarbons due to PAHs destruction does not appear to be an efficient route here, as PAHs are not commonly observed in low-mass protostellar systems (Geers et al. 2009), and the UV-fields required for this process are above 10 [3] (Abergel et al. 2003).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Thermal desorption of COMs in the S68N outflow (rejected because dust temperatures at a few 10^3 au are well below COM desorption temperatures and there is no enhancement closer to the source).

evidence.quote: Thermal desorption of molecules from grains is not likely as dust temperatures at distances of few times 10 [3] au from the protostar are well below the desorption temperatures for most COMs.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Accretion shock origin for SO in TMC1 (ruled out by narrow linewidths, pointing instead to emission along the cavity walls).

evidence.quote: However, narrow linewidths of SO toward TMC1 seem to rule out the accretion shock scenario, and points to emission along the cavity walls (Harsono et al. 2021).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Warm carbon-chain chemistry (WCCC) to explain C2H and c-C3H2 (rejected in favor of PDR chemistry in UV-irradiated outflow cavity walls).

evidence.loc: 4.6. Carbon-chains and other hydrocarbons vs COMs
evidence.quote: Both c-C 3 H 2 and C 2 H can be solely explained by PDR chemistry (Guzmán et al. 2015; Cuadrado et al. 2015) even in moderate UV fields of low-mass protostars and therefore WCCC chemistry does not need to be invoked for the sources presented in this work.

limitations_admitted.value: Spatial and kinematic resolution is insufficient to confirm Keplerian rotation for Class 0 embedded disks (such as SMM3).

evidence.quote: While we assume that this compact emission belongs to the young, embedded disk, we do not have spatial and kinematic resolution to confirm the presence of Class 0 Keplerian disks in our sample.
However, to unambiguously identify the disk and its radius, higher spatial and spectral resolution data are necessary.

limitations_admitted.value: ALMA 12m observations resolve out large-scale envelope emission (MRS ~ 5''), and primary beam (~30'') does not capture the entirety of the outflows.

evidence.quote: Thus, the sub-arcsecond ALMA 12m array observations tend to resolve-out the envelope emission.
In all cases, we do not capture the entirety of the outflows as they extend beyond the primary beam of observations (∼ 30 [′′] ).

limitations_admitted.value: H2CCO 13_1,13-12_1,12 and NH2CHO 12_2,10-12_2,10 in S68N are only 4 km s^-1 apart and possibly blended; more low-energy transitions are required to confirm line identification.

evidence.quote: it is possible that those lines are blended. More lowenergy transitions would be required to confirm the identification of these lines.

limitations_admitted.value: Lack of an optically thin CH3OH isotopologue detection in the S68N outflow leads to large uncertainties in outflow COM abundance ratios.

evidence.loc: 4.5. COMs in outflow versus hot core
evidence.quote: noting that due to lack of optically thin CH 3 OH line detected in the outflow, our uncertainties are larger.

limitations_admitted.value: In B1-c, methanol emission in the outflow overlaps with high-velocity SO emission, preventing precise outflow abundance measurements.

evidence.loc: 4.5. COMs in outflow versus hot core
evidence.quote: B1-c - another source with an outflow containing ice mantle products, has methanol lines overlapping with the high-velocity SO outflow, therefore precise abundance measurements are not possible.

referee_caveats_inferred: Appendix A (pages 22-24), which is supposed to contain Table A.1 (observational details) and Table A.2 (targeted molecular transitions and detections), is completely blank in the manuscript PDF, omitting critical observational metadata and line frequencies.
The analysis is primarily a qualitative morphological overview across heterogeneous datasets with different spectral coverages, meaning not all molecules were observed toward all 16 sources.
Column densities in the S68N outflow are derived from single transitions assuming a fixed excitation temperature of 20 K and LTE, which may suffer from sub-thermal excitation effects.

reproducibility.score_reason: All six ALMA project codes are explicitly stated and public, and the moment 0 velocity integration ranges and CASSIS LTE assumptions (Tex=20 K, FWHM=3 km/s) are given, but Appendix A (Tables A.1 and A.2) is blank in the manuscript and calibration/imaging recipes are deferred to companion papers.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: The paper's main contribution is a qualitative morphological classification (Table 2, Fig. 11) rather than quantitative measurements, and the essential observational tables (A.1, A.2) are missing from the manuscript.
